chapter_title: Introduction to AWS Systems Manager (SSM) for DevOps
chapter_summary:
Welcome to the foundational chapter on AWS Systems Manager (SSM), a powerful and versatile service that acts as the "Swiss Army knife" for operational management in AWS. For a DevOps professional, SSM is indispensable for automating routine tasks, maintaining configuration compliance, and gaining deep operational insights across a fleet of EC2 instances, on-premises servers, and even virtual machines in other cloud environments. SSM centralizes operational data and provides a unified interface to view and act on your operational issues, drastically reducing the need for manual intervention and improving the consistency and reliability of your infrastructure.

At its core, SSM operates by deploying an SSM Agent on your managed instances. This agent is pre-installed on many Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) and can be manually installed on others. The agent communicates with the SSM service using a secure, encrypted channel, allowing the service to send commands and receive status updates. This agent-based architecture means that SSM can manage instances without requiring SSH access or open inbound ports, significantly enhancing security posture. Imagine needing to patch hundreds of servers; traditionally, this would involve scripting SSH commands, managing credentials, and handling potential failures. With SSM, you can initiate a patch operation from a central console or API, and the agents on each instance will execute the necessary steps, reporting back their status. This shift from reactive, manual operations to proactive, automated management is a cornerstone of modern DevOps practices.

SSM encompasses a wide array of capabilities, each designed to address specific operational challenges. For instance, `Run Command` allows you to execute shell scripts or PowerShell commands on a fleet of instances simultaneously, ideal for ad-hoc troubleshooting or deploying small configuration changes. `State Manager` takes this a step further by defining a desired state for your instances and continuously enforcing it, ensuring that your servers always conform to your specified configurations. This is critical for preventing configuration drift, where instances gradually deviate from their intended state over time due to manual changes or unmanaged updates. By using State Manager, you can ensure that all your web servers, for example, have the same version of Apache installed and configured identically, leading to more predictable application behavior.

Another crucial aspect of SSM is its ability to integrate with other AWS services, forming a comprehensive operational ecosystem. For example, SSM can publish operational data to Amazon CloudWatch, allowing you to monitor the health and performance of your instances and trigger alarms based on predefined metrics. It can also integrate with AWS Security Hub for security findings and AWS Config for compliance auditing. This interconnectedness means that SSM isn't just a standalone tool; it's a central hub that orchestrates various operational tasks and provides a holistic view of your infrastructure's health and compliance. Understanding how to leverage these integrations is key to building robust, automated, and secure DevOps pipelines.

Common mistakes often include not correctly configuring IAM roles for SSM agents, leading to permission denied errors when attempting to execute commands. Always ensure your EC2 instances have an IAM instance profile attached with the `AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore` policy, or a custom policy granting necessary SSM permissions. Another pitfall is assuming SSM works without an agent; remember, the agent is the bridge. Safety notes include being cautious with `Run Command` on production instances, especially when executing commands that modify system files or services. Always test commands in a staging environment first and use rate controls and error thresholds to minimize blast radius during large-scale deployments. By embracing SSM, you're not just automating tasks; you're building a more resilient, secure, and efficient operational backbone for your AWS infrastructure.

narration.text: In this lesson we will meet AWS Systems Manager, the operations hub many teams use to automate repetitive tasks, enforce consistent configurations, and troubleshoot systems securely. Think of SSM as a Swiss Army knife: a single service with focused capabilities — like running commands, enforcing desired states, and executing automation workflows — that together reduce manual toil across EC2 instances and other managed servers. You will learn how the SSM Agent acts as the secure bridge between your instances and the SSM control plane, why removing direct SSH access improves security, and how SSM integrates with monitoring and compliance tools to create a cohesive operational surface. I'll point out common pitfalls you should avoid, such as missing IAM instance profiles or forgetting to start the agent, and we'll walk through a hands-on activity where you launch an instance, confirm the agent, and run a simple script remotely. By the end of this chapter you will understand when to reach for Run Command, when to declare a desired state with State Manager, and how Automation Documents let you codify multi-step operations. Consider: what operations in your environment would you centralize first with SSM?

screens.title: What is AWS Systems Manager (SSM)?
screens.subtitle: A definition and practical framing for DevOps teams

narration.text: AWS Systems Manager is a collection of capabilities designed to automate operational tasks across EC2 instances, on-premises servers, and compatible virtual machines. In practical terms, SSM centralizes operational data and exposes a unified control plane so you can run commands, enforce configurations, and orchestrate multi-step procedures without individually logging into servers. For a DevOps practitioner, the crucial benefit is the shift from reactive, manual fixes to proactive, codified operations. For example, instead of running ad-hoc SSH scripts on dozens of servers to update a package, you can use SSM Run Command to execute a single documented command that runs across the fleet and returns structured output. One common misconception is that SSM replaces configuration management entirely; instead, it complements those tools by providing mechanisms for enforcement, ad-hoc operations, and automation documents that integrate with other services. The concept card shows SSM as the hub connecting agents, automation, state enforcement, and monitoring. Remember: SSM organizes and automates operational work; it does not remove the need for well-defined configurations, testing, and staged rollouts. How would centralizing a frequent operational task improve safety and speed in your environment?

keyIdea.title: SSM centralizes operations
keyIdea.text: SSM is a unified set of tools for automating and observing operational work, reducing manual, error-prone intervention across many systems.

content.html:
Core Concept

What is SSM?

A unified service for automating operational tasks across managed servers and instances, providing commands, state enforcement, and automation workflows.

Quick metaphor

Think of SSM as a control plane and toolkit — like a remote operations console — that talks to each instance through an installed agent.

Key Takeaway

SSM reduces manual interventions by centralizing execution, reporting, and enforcement across your infrastructure.

Definition
SSM = Run Command + State Manager + Automation + Agent + Integrations
Run Command

Execute scripts or commands on instances at scale for ad-hoc tasks or triage.

State Manager

Declare desired systems state and enforce it to prevent configuration drift.

Automation

Chain and schedule multi-step operations using documents.

Misconception

SSM is not a silver bullet that replaces all configuration management. It complements other tools by enforcing and automating specific operational tasks.

Example

Use Run Command to push a quick package update across 50 web servers and return a single report of success or failure for each host, avoiding manual SSH sessions.

screens.title: SSM Agent: the secure bridge
screens.subtitle: How the agent communicates and why it improves security

narration.text: The SSM Agent is the lightweight piece of software that runs on each managed instance and enables SSM to execute commands, apply configurations, and report results. The agent opens an outbound encrypted channel to the SSM service, which means you rarely need inbound ports like SSH. This design improves security posture because you can remove or avoid exposing SSH entirely for management tasks. A concrete example: when you run a patch job via SSM, the control plane sends the operation to each agent; each agent performs the work locally and sends back structured status. A common mistake is assuming the agent is always present — some custom AMIs omit it or it may be stopped. Always verify the agent is running and that your instance has an IAM instance profile with the necessary SSM permissions. Another misconception is that the agent provides full remote shell parity with SSH; it exposes command execution and managed features, but not a persistent interactive shell. Key checks for reliability include confirming the agent service status, verifying instance registration in the Systems Manager console, and ensuring outbound connectivity to the SSM endpoints. How will you verify agent health in your environment?

keyIdea.title: Agent-first management
keyIdea.text: The SSM Agent provides secure, outbound-only communication enabling remote operations without opening inbound management ports like SSH.

content.html:
Definition

SSM Agent

A process on managed instances that receives instructions from Systems Manager, executes them, and reports status back securely.

Outbound encrypted channel

No inbound ports required for management commands.

Status reporting

Agents return structured results and exit codes for central analysis.

Common mistake

Assuming the agent is installed and running on custom AMIs. Always confirm installation and service status before relying on SSM for management.

Key Takeaway

The agent is the bridge — without it, SSM cannot manage the instance. Verify agent presence and correct IAM role to enable management.

Agent checks and diagnostics
  • Confirm the agent service is running on the instance and set to start automatically.
  • Ensure the instance is visible in the Systems Manager > Managed instances list after boot.
  • Verify the IAM instance profile grants SSM permissions, such as AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore or equivalent.
  • Check outbound network access to SSM endpoints if the instance is in a restricted subnet.
Example scenario

You launch an EC2 from a custom AMI and it does not appear in Managed instances. First check the IAM instance profile, then confirm the agent service is installed and running. If either is missing, the instance won't register and SSM commands will fail.

screens.title: Run Command: execute at scale
screens.subtitle: How to run ad-hoc scripts and gather results from a fleet

narration.text: Run Command is SSM's capability for executing shell or PowerShell commands remotely on one or many managed instances. Use it for ad-hoc troubleshooting, quick configuration changes, and incident response when you need immediate action across multiple hosts. The typical process is: author or select a command document like AWS-RunShellScript, pick target instances, provide the script or commands, and run. Each agent executes the commands locally and streams the output back to the control plane so you can inspect results per host. A concrete example: apply a short diagnostic script that writes a line to a temporary file and lists it, then view the resulting output for each instance. Important safety notes: do not run destructive commands on production without staging; use rate controls and error thresholds when targeting large fleets to reduce blast radius; and always validate IAM permissions, because otherwise commands fail with a permission denied state. A common misconception is that Run Command gives you an interactive shell — it does not. It is a remote execution mechanism designed for orchestration and repeatability. After you run a command, inspect success, standard output, and exit codes to confirm each host's state.

keyIdea.title: Remote execution with reporting
keyIdea.text: Run Command provides fleet-wide execution and structured output, enabling rapid troubleshooting and controlled changes without SSH.

content.html:
Process Flow

Run Command steps

  1. Choose a command document such as AWS-RunShellScript.
  2. Provide the shell or PowerShell script to execute.
  3. Select target instances by tags or manually.
  4. Run with rate controls if needed and monitor output per instance.
Misconception check

Run Command is not an interactive shell. It executes provided commands and returns their output for inspection.

Common-mistake

Running untested commands at fleet scale without rate limits can produce widespread failures.

Concrete example
#!/bin/bash
echo "Hello from SSM Run Command on $(hostname)!" > /tmp/ssm_hello.txt
cat /tmp/ssm_hello.txt
ls -l /tmp/ssm_hello.txt
What to observe

Per-instance output includes printed lines and file listing. Command status shows Success or Failed.

Safety tip

Run in staging first, then apply rate controls and thresholds when scaling to production.

Key Takeaway

Use Run Command for repeatable, auditable, remote execution with structured outputs and status for each host.

screens.title: State Manager vs. Run Command
screens.subtitle: When to enforce desired state and when to run ad-hoc commands

narration.text: Understanding the difference between State Manager and Run Command prevents using the wrong tool for the job. Run Command is ideal for one-off or ad-hoc operations: diagnostics, quick fixes, or emergency remediation where immediate execution is required. State Manager is for declaring a desired configuration and continuously enforcing it, preventing drift over time. For instance, if you need to ensure every web server always has a specific package and configuration present, declare that using State Manager and the system will periodically check and correct drift. A common mistake is using Run Command repeatedly to fix drift; this creates manual repeatability rather than a declarative solution. Conversely, using State Manager to execute short-lived diagnostic scripts does not match its intended use of maintaining long-term configuration. Each tool has a role: Run Command for episodic control and State Manager for persistent enforcement. When designing operational patterns, prefer State Manager for consistency guarantees and Run Command for immediate triage and rapid remediation. To test your choice, ask whether the change should persist automatically or is a single corrective action. State Manager vs. Run Command means run command for ad-hoc actions; state manager for continuous enforcement of a declared desired state.. In practical terms, when to enforce desired state and when to run ad-hoc commands. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Use the right tool
keyIdea.text: Run Command for ad-hoc actions; State Manager for continuous enforcement of a declared desired state.

content.html:
Comparison

Run Command vs State Manager

Run Command
  • Ad-hoc execution
  • Immediate remediation or diagnostics
  • Per-instance output and status
State Manager
  • Declare desired state
  • Continuous enforcement
  • Prevents configuration drift
Misconception

Using Run Command as a repeated band-aid for drift is brittle. Use State Manager or configuration tools to maintain long-term consistency.

Scenario

Your team notices that a package on web servers sometimes gets updated manually, producing drift. Choose State Manager to declare the desired package version and schedule periodic enforcement, rather than repeatedly running a corrective script via Run Command.

Check your understanding

If a change should be permanent and automatically corrected when drift occurs, which tool do you use? (Answer: State Manager.)

Key Takeaway

Match Run Command to episodic tasks and State Manager to declarative, persistent configuration enforcement.

screens.title: Automation Documents and Workflows
screens.subtitle: Codify multi-step operational tasks into reusable documents

narration.text: Automation Documents let you codify complex, multi-step operational workflows into a repeatable and auditable form. An Automation Document can include steps such as stopping a service, applying a patch, validating the change, and then notifying other systems. For DevOps, this means less manual orchestration and clearer runbooks that can be executed against single instances or entire fleets. A concrete use case is an automated patching run: the document defines patch targets, pre-checks, patch application, and a post-check to confirm success. Unlike a one-off Run Command, Automation Documents are designed to be safe, idempotent where possible, and composable. A common misconception is that Automation Documents are only for complex operations. In practice, start by turning frequent manual sequences into documents — even small sequences benefit from reproducibility and logs. When authoring an Automation Document, think about error handling, rollback steps, and observability: include meaningful outputs and status checks so you can programmatically decide next steps or trigger alarms. How could you convert a team's manual runbook into an Automation Document to reduce on-call friction? Automation Documents and Workflows means automation documents convert manual multi-step tasks into reusable, auditable workflows that support error handling and notification.. In practical terms, codify multi-step operational tasks into reusable documents. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Codified runbooks
keyIdea.text: Automation Documents convert manual multi-step tasks into reusable, auditable workflows that support error handling and notification.

content.html:
Definition

Automation Documents

Declarative documents describing ordered steps, inputs, and outputs for operational tasks, which SSM can execute and track.

Example: Patching workflow
  1. Run pre-checks to confirm instance readiness.
  2. Install patches and restart services as required.
  3. Run post-checks and report results to monitoring and compliance systems.
Design tips
  • Include clear inputs and outputs for each step.
  • Design idempotent actions when possible.
  • Specify error handling and rollback paths.
Analogy

Think of an Automation Document as a tested runbook that the system can execute reliably, with logs and status for each step.

Key Takeaway

Automate repetitive sequences into documents to reduce manual error and capture clear audit trails.

screens.title: Managed Instances & Inventory
screens.subtitle: What qualifies as a managed instance and how SSM inventories resources

narration.text: A managed instance is any server or virtual machine that runs the SSM Agent and is configured to communicate with the Systems Manager service. That includes EC2 instances, on-premises servers, and VMs in other clouds provided the agent is installed and network access allows outbound communication. Once registered, an instance appears in SSM's Managed Instances view and can be targeted by Run Command, State Manager, and Automation Documents. SSM can also collect inventory about installed packages and configuration, helping you track compliance and create targeted operations. A frequent operational question is how to include non-AWS servers: install the agent, ensure proper IAM or registration, and configure access to SSM endpoints. Misconceptions often arise around the need for public IPs; outbound connectivity from private subnets to SSM endpoints is sufficient when routes and VPC endpoints are configured. The practical takeaway is: verify an instance shows up in the Managed Instances list before relying on it for automation. That list is your authoritative inventory for SSM-managed hosts. Managed Instances & Inventory means any server with the ssm agent and correct registration becomes manageable through ssm and participates in inventory and automation.. In practical terms, what qualifies as a managed instance and how ssm inventories resources. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Managed instance = agent + registration
keyIdea.text: Any server with the SSM Agent and correct registration becomes manageable through SSM and participates in inventory and automation.

content.html:
Definition

Managed Instance

An instance running the SSM Agent and registered with Systems Manager. Appears in Managed Instances and is eligible for operations and inventory collection.

Inventory & use

SSM can gather package lists and configuration data to help you target operations and prove compliance across your fleet.

Practical checks
  • Confirm the instance appears under Systems Manager > Managed Instances after boot.
  • Ensure agent is installed and running on custom AMIs or on-premises servers.
  • Verify network routes or endpoints allow outbound SSM connectivity from private networks.
Example

An on-premises VM is turned into a managed instance after installing the SSM Agent and completing registration. It can then be targeted just like an EC2 instance for commands and state enforcement.

narration.text: IAM instance profiles grant the instance the permissions it needs to interact with Systems Manager. The managed policy AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore covers the typical permissions required for the SSM Agent to register, send status, and allow Run Command execution. A common operational failure is launching an instance without an attached instance profile or with insufficient permissions, which prevents registration and leads to permission denied errors when you attempt commands. When using custom policies, ensure the agent can put logs, send inventory, and access SSM endpoints. Importantly, the agent acts using the instance role, so you should audit roles and permissions systematically and avoid embedding long-lived credentials on the instance. One misconception is that SSM can operate without any role — it cannot. If an instance does not have the necessary permissions, SSM may fail silently until you check registration and logs. Best practice: attach a role with least-privilege permissions needed for SSM functionality and validate by confirming the instance appears as managed and can successfully run a simple test command. IAM Instance Profiles for SSM means attach an iam instance profile with ssm permissions to enable the agent to register, report status, and execute commands securely.. In practical terms, permissions required and common pitfalls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Role-driven agent permissions
keyIdea.text: Attach an IAM instance profile with SSM permissions to enable the agent to register, report status, and execute commands securely.

content.html:
Definition

IAM Instance Profile

An IAM role attached to an EC2 instance that grants the SSM Agent permission to call Systems Manager APIs and related services.

Checklist
  • Attach AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore or equivalent.
  • Confirm role allows sending logs and inventory when needed.
  • Use least privilege and avoid embedding long-lived credentials.
Common pitfalls
  • No instance profile attached at launch — instance will not register as managed.
  • Custom policy missing specific SSM permissions results in permission denied during commands.
  • Assuming SSM works without a role — it relies on role-based permissions.
Example

Launch an EC2 with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore attached. If it does not appear in Managed instances, verify the role and agent service are both present.

screens.title: SSM integrations: Monitoring and compliance
screens.subtitle: How SSM connects to CloudWatch, Security Hub, and AWS Config

narration.text: SSM does not operate in isolation — it commonly integrates with CloudWatch, AWS Config, and security services to provide a fuller operational picture. For monitoring, SSM can publish command status and metrics to CloudWatch, letting you create alarms and dashboards based on success rates or error counts. For compliance, SSM inventory and State Manager evaluation can feed AWS Config so auditors see whether instances conform to expected configurations. Security Hub can receive findings triggered by automation or SSM-driven checks, creating a consolidated view of security posture. A practical example: configure State Manager to enforce a required patch level and send noncompliance records to AWS Config; if a patch fails repeatedly, trigger an alarm in CloudWatch and run an Automation Document to remediate. A common misconception is that these integrations happen automatically — you must configure the flows and ensure roles permit cross-service actions. The main operational benefit is that SSM acts as a source of truth for both operations and compliance, allowing automated remediation and observable audit trails. SSM integrations: Monitoring and compliance means ssm integrates with monitoring and compliance services so automated actions are observable and auditable across your environment.. In practical terms, how ssm connects to cloudwatch, security hub, and aws config. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: SSM as an operational hub
keyIdea.text: SSM integrates with monitoring and compliance services so automated actions are observable and auditable across your environment.

content.html:
Integration

Monitoring and Compliance

SSM publishes operational results and inventory that other services can consume for alerts, dashboards, and audits.

CloudWatch

Track command success/failure, build alarms, and create dashboards.

AWS Config

Use inventory and state evaluations for compliance reporting.

Security Hub

Aggregate security findings related to operational checks and remediations.

Example workflow

State Manager reports noncompliance to AWS Config. Config triggers an alert or workflow that runs an Automation Document to remediate, while CloudWatch tracks the remediation metrics.

Practical note

Enable and configure each integration explicitly. Ensure cross-service permissions are granted to allow data flow and action execution.

Key Takeaway

Integrate SSM with monitoring and compliance systems to turn operational actions into observable, auditable events.

screens.title: Verify SSM Agent and run a basic command
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step lab walkthrough using the provided demo script

narration.text: This walkthrough follows the hands-on activity: launch an EC2 instance, confirm the agent, and run a basic Run Command script. First, when launching your instance choose an Amazon Linux 2 AMI which typically has the SSM Agent pre-installed. Attach an IAM instance profile with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy. Important: do not open SSH ports; SSM can manage the instance without them. After the instance boots, open Systems Manager > Managed instances and wait for the new host to appear. If it does not, verify the instance profile and that the agent service is running. Next, navigate to Systems Manager > Run Command, choose the AWS-RunShellScript document, and paste the test script into the commands section. The script writes a line to /tmp/ssm_hello. txt, prints it, and lists the file. Run the command targeting your instance, and after it completes, open the Command ID details and inspect the Output tab. You should see the greeting and file details; a success status confirms the agent can execute commands. If the status shows permission denied or the instance is not listed, re-check the role and agent status. This exercise demonstrates secure remote execution without SSH and validates the SSM control flow in your environment.

keyIdea.title: Lab verification
keyIdea.text: Confirm the SSM Agent is present, the instance has the correct IAM profile, and Run Command returns expected output to validate setup.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity

Verify Agent & Run Command

Follow these high-level steps exactly as written to validate SSM configuration and then execute the demo script.
  1. Launch an EC2 using Amazon Linux 2 and attach an IAM instance profile with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore.
  2. Do not open SSH in the security group; SSM manages the host outbound-only.
  3. Confirm the instance appears in Systems Manager > Managed instances.
  4. Run the AWS-RunShellScript command targeting the instance with the demo script below.
  5. Open the Command ID and check the Output tab for expected text and file listing.
Troubleshoot

If not appearing: verify the IAM role, verify the agent service is installed and running, and confirm outbound access to SSM endpoints or VPC endpoints for Systems Manager.

#!/bin/bash
echo "Hello from SSM Run Command on $(hostname)!" > /tmp/ssm_hello.txt
cat /tmp/ssm_hello.txt
ls -l /tmp/ssm_hello.txt
Expected output

Standard output should include the greeting line and the file listing. Command status should report Success for the target instance.

Key Takeaway

This activity proves the agent and role are functioning and that you can execute remote commands securely without SSH.

screens.title: Operational safety and common mistakes
screens.subtitle: Patterns to reduce blast radius and ensure predictable outcomes

narration.text: Operational safety with SSM requires deliberate patterns: test in staging, use rate controls, define error thresholds, and verify outputs. A common mistake is running powerful scripts across the entire fleet without limiting concurrency, which creates a large blast radius for mistakes. Instead, target small groups, confirm success, and gradually expand. Another frequent error is forgetting to attach an IAM instance profile, which results in registration failures — always verify the instance appears in Managed Instances before running corrective actions. Safety also includes thinking about rollback: build Automation Documents that include post-checks and, where possible, rollback steps. For compliance, ensure State Manager declarations are auditable and that inventory data is shipped to AWS Config or your compliance system. In incident response, prefer Run Command for immediate triage, but record all outputs and turn successful remediation into an Automation Document for repeatability. Lastly, log and monitor everything you run through CloudWatch so you can detect and alert on anomalous failure patterns. What small step can you take today to reduce risk when running SSM at scale? content.html:
Best Practice

Safety patterns for SSM

  • Test in staging and validate outputs before production runs.
  • Use rate controls and batch operations to limit blast radius.
  • Define error thresholds and automatic halting behavior.
  • Record outputs and integrate with CloudWatch and Config for audits.
Common mistakes

Running untested scripts at scale, missing instance profiles, and assuming the agent is present are recurring causes of failure. Avoid them with small tests and checks.

Pro tip

After a successful ad-hoc Run Command remediation, convert it into an Automation Document so the runbook becomes repeatable, auditable, and safer for future incidents.

Key Takeaway

Design workflows that limit impact, include verification steps, and convert manual fixes into automated documents to improve reliability and auditability.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's wrap up the most important ideas to carry forward. First, AWS Systems Manager is a unified toolkit that centralizes operational tasks, enabling fleet-wide actions without SSH when the SSM Agent is present. Second, the SSM Agent runs on each managed host, uses outbound encrypted channels, and relies on the instance's IAM profile to operate. Third, Run Command is for ad-hoc execution and quick remediation, while State Manager enforces a desired configuration continuously. Also remember Automation Documents for codifying multi-step runbooks, and that integrations with CloudWatch and AWS Config make operations observable and auditable. A few practical checks: verify the agent is running, confirm instances appear in the Managed Instances list, and ensure the correct IAM instance profile is attached. Finally, adopt safety patterns: test in staging, use rate limits, and convert manual fixes into automated, auditable procedures. screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders for operational use

narration.text: As a final quick reference, keep three compact reminders. First, always verify the SSM Agent and that the instance is registered before relying on SSM for any operations. Second, attach an IAM instance profile with the correct permissions — without it, commands fail. Third, pick the correct capability: use Run Command for immediate, single-run actions, State Manager for continuous enforcement, and Automation Documents to codify multi-step runbooks. These three checks will prevent the most common failures and help you run safer, more auditable operations. Before you finish, choose one operational task in your environment to move into SSM — maybe a diagnostic script you currently run manually — and convert it into either a Run Command or an Automation Document so you can measure the time and errors you save.
